OCCUPATION-SPECIFIC OVERTIME EXEMPTION RULES FOR PHYSICIANS, REGISTERED NURSES, PHARMACISTS, AND PRIVATE-SCHOOL TEACHERS (LAB. CODE §§ 514, 515(F), 515.6, 515.8; WAGE ORDER 5-2001, § 1(B)(3)) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Valley Medical Group, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Valley Medical Group, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe the occupation-specific overtime rules that California's Labor Code and the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders lay over the general professional exemption — the body of law that governs a position such as Staff Physician, held by Jordan Lee.

It describes the daily and weekly overtime requirement in Labor Code section 510 and the authority in section 515(a) under which the Industrial Welfare Commission establishes the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions; the separate hourly-rate exemption for licensed physicians and surgeons in section 515.6, the annual adjustment mechanism written into that section, and the rate the Department of Industrial Relations has most recently published under it; the two categories section 515.6 expressly does not reach, namely employees in a medical internship or resident program and physicians covered by a collective bargaining agreement meeting the conditions of section 514; section 515(f)'s rule that a registered nurse employed to engage in the practice of nursing is not exempted under the wage orders unless the nurse individually meets the executive or administrative criteria, and the three advanced-practice-nurse categories that rule does not apply to; the parallel provision in section 1(B)(3) of Wage Order 5-2001, which states the same rule for pharmacists employed to engage in the practice of pharmacy; and the separate exemption in section 515.8 for teachers at private elementary and secondary schools, with its duties requirements, its salary floor measured against public school district salary schedules, its degree-or-credential requirement, and the occupations it excludes.

This information sheet describes the law. It does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, does not evaluate any particular job or set of duties, does not calculate any employee's pay or overtime, and does not file anything with any agency or court.

THE OVERTIME REQUIREMENT AND THE GENERAL EXEMPTION AUTHORITY THESE RULES SIT ON TOP OF
California law requires overtime compensation for work beyond eight hours in a workday and beyond 40 hours in a workweek, and for the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in a workweek, at no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay, with a double-time requirement for work beyond 12 hours in a day (Labor Code section 510(a)).

Labor Code section 515(a) is the provision under which the Industrial Welfare Commission may establish exemptions from that requirement for executive, administrative, and professional employees, and by its terms it permits those exemptions only where the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment.

The provisions described in the rest of this document are occupation-specific rules that sit on top of that general framework. Two of them — sections 515.6 and 515.8 — are stand-alone statutory exemptions that state their own criteria and, by their own terms, make section 510 inapplicable to a defined group of employees. The others run the other direction: Labor Code section 515(f) and section 1(B)(3)(f) of Wage Order 5-2001 state that particular licensed occupations are not covered by the professional exemption at all unless the employee separately meets the executive or administrative criteria.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Eight hours of labor constitutes a day’s work. Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee. Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 510(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  "(a) The Industrial Welfare Commission may establish exemptions from the requirement that an overtime rate of compensation be paid pursuant to Sections 510 and 511 for executive, administrative, and professional employees, if the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.)
  Known gap: This clause states the framework only. It does not describe the duties tests for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions themselves, which appear in the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders rather than in section 515, and which this corpus addresses in a separate document on the "primarily engaged in" duties test; nor does it describe the separate computer software employee exemption of Labor Code section 515.5, which is the subject of its own document in this corpus. Which of the Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders applies to a given employee turns on the employer's industry or the employee's occupation, a question this document does not address. Labor Code section 510(a) contains further provisions that are not quoted here, including its exceptions for alternative workweek schedules adopted under sections 511, 514, and 554 and its rule that an employer need not combine more than one rate of overtime compensation; the section 510(a) quotation below collapses the double spacing the posted text uses between sentences.

THE LICENSED PHYSICIAN AND SURGEON EXEMPTION (LABOR CODE SECTION 515.6)
Labor Code section 515.6(a) states that section 510 does not apply to an employee who satisfies three conditions at once: the employee is a licensed physician or surgeon; the employee is primarily engaged in duties that require licensure under the Medical Practice Act, which the statute identifies as Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 2000) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code; and the employee's hourly rate of pay is equal to or greater than a dollar threshold that the statute prints as fifty-five dollars ($55.00).

Two features distinguish this exemption from the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions described in section 515(a). First, its pay component is an hourly rate of pay rather than a monthly salary, and it is a fixed dollar figure rather than a multiple of the state minimum wage. Second, the statute contains its own escalator: the same subdivision directs the Department of Industrial Relations to adjust the threshold rate of pay each October 1, effective the following January 1, by an amount equal to the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. The figure actually in force is therefore the department's most recently published adjusted figure, not the $55.00 printed in the code; the next clause of this document reports that published figure as of the date this document was verified.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "515.6. (a) Section 510 shall not apply to any employee who is a licensed physician or surgeon, who is primarily engaged in duties that require licensure pursuant to Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 2000) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code, and whose hourly rate of pay is equal to or greater than fifty-five dollars ($55.00)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.6(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.6.)
  "The department shall adjust this threshold rate of pay each October 1, to be effective the following January 1, by an amount equal to the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.6(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.6(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.6.)
  Known gap: The $55.00 figure quoted below is the base amount that appears in the codified text; it is not the operative threshold today, because subdivision (a) requires annual adjustment and the Department of Industrial Relations publishes the adjusted figure separately. Section 515.6 by its terms makes only section 510 inapplicable; this clause does not address the effect, if any, of the exemption on other Labor Code provisions or on any provision of an applicable wage order, and it does not address whether a physician who does not meet section 515.6 might separately fall within an exemption established by the Industrial Welfare Commission under section 515(a). Whether particular duties "require licensure" under the Business and Professions Code chapter the statute names, and whether an individual is "primarily engaged" in them, are questions of fact that this document does not apply to any position, including the position of Staff Physician.

THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS' MOST RECENTLY PUBLISHED PHYSICIAN RATE
The Department of Industrial Relations publishes the dollar figure that results from the annual adjustment section 515.6(a) requires. As of the date this clause was verified, the department's own published notice states that, in accordance with Labor Code section 515.6(a), it adjusted the licensed physicians and surgeons employee's minimum hourly rate of pay exemption from $103.75 to $107.17 effective January 1, 2026, reflecting a 3.3 percent increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. The same notice records that the figure in force for the preceding year was $103.75, effective January 1, 2025, and that the department measured the 3.3 percent change from an August 2024 index value of 331.734 to an August 2025 index value of 342.673.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In accordance with Labor Code Section 515.6(a), the department has adjusted the licensed physicians and surgeons employee’s minimum hourly rate of pay exemption from $103.75 to $107.17 effective January 1, 2026, reflecting the 3.3% increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers."
  — California Department of Industrial Relations, Overtime Exemption for Licensed Physicians and Surgeons (Office of the Director – Research, effective January 1, 2026), California Department of Industrial Relations (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/Physicians.htm)
  "One of the criteria is that the employee’s hourly rate of pay is not less than fifty-five dollars ($55.00), effective January 1, 2002. The Department of Industrial Relations is responsible for adjusting this pay rate on October 1st of each year to be effective on January 1st of the following year by an amount equal to the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Last year, the department adjusted the rate to $103.75, effective January 1, 2025."
  — California Department of Industrial Relations, Overtime Exemption for Licensed Physicians and Surgeons (Office of the Director – Research, effective January 1, 2026), California Department of Industrial Relations (https://www.dir.ca.gov/OPRL/Physicians.htm)
  Known gap: This clause reports the figures the Department of Industrial Relations published as of the checkedDate above, taken from the department's own webpage rather than from the codified statutory text, which prints only the $55.00 base figure covered in the preceding clause. By the statute's own mechanism the department recalculates and republishes the figure each October for the following January 1, so a later adjustment will supersede the figure quoted here, and this document's text does not update itself as new figures are published. The department's page is a single-source publication: it was fetched twice through independent request paths for this verification, but no second publisher of the adjusted figure was used. The clause reports the published rate and does not compute or compare any individual's rate of pay.

WHO THE PHYSICIAN EXEMPTION DOES NOT REACH: INTERNS, RESIDENTS, AND EMPLOYEES UNDER A SECTION 514 AGREEMENT
Labor Code section 515.6(b) places two categories outside the exemption created by subdivision (a). The first is an employee employed in a medical internship or resident program. The second is a physician employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement pursuant to section 514.

Section 514 is a separate exemption of general application. It provides that sections 510 and 511 do not apply to an employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement where the agreement expressly provides for the wages, hours of work, and working conditions of the employees, where the agreement provides premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked, and where the agreement provides a regular hourly rate of pay for those employees of not less than 30 percent more than the state minimum wage. A physician employee who falls within section 514 is therefore outside section 510 by operation of section 514 itself, and section 515.6(b) states that the section 515.6 exemption does not apply to that employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "(b) The exemption provided in subdivision (a) shall not apply to an employee employed in a medical internship or resident program or to a physician employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement pursuant to Section 514."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.6(b) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.6(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.6.)
  "514. Sections 510 and 511 do not apply to an employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement if the agreement expressly provides for the wages, hours of work, and working conditions of the employees, and if the agreement provides premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked and a regular hourly rate of pay for those employees of not less than 30 percent more than the state minimum wage."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 514 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 514 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=514.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the two exclusions in the text of section 515.6(b) and the conditions section 514 states. It does not evaluate whether any particular training program is "a medical internship or resident program" within the meaning of the statute, and it does not evaluate whether any particular collective bargaining agreement satisfies each of the conditions section 514 lists — questions that depend on the terms of the agreement and the facts of the employment. Section 514 applies to employees generally and is not limited to physicians; its interaction with alternative workweek schedules under section 510(a)(2) is not described here. The section 515.6(b) quotation below joins a line break that falls inside the phrase "medical internship or resident program" in the posted text.

REGISTERED NURSES ARE NOT EXEMPT AS PROFESSIONAL EMPLOYEES (LABOR CODE SECTION 515(F)(1))
Labor Code section 515(f)(1) addresses registered nurses directly. It states that, in addition to the requirements of subdivision (a), a registered nurse employed to engage in the practice of nursing is not exempted from coverage under the orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission unless the nurse individually meets the criteria for exemptions established for executive or administrative employees.

The structure of that sentence matters. It does not create an exemption; it closes one. A registered nurse who is employed to engage in the practice of nursing cannot be treated as an exempt professional employee on the strength of the nursing license and nursing duties alone. The only route to exempt status the subdivision leaves open is the executive or administrative route, and it requires that the individual nurse meet those criteria — which, under section 515(a), include being primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercising discretion and independent judgment, and earning the required salary.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "(f) (1) In addition to the requirements of subdivision (a), a registered nurse employed to engage in the practice of nursing shall not be exempted from coverage under the orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, unless he or she individually meets the criteria for exemptions established for executive or administrative employees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515(f)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the text of section 515(f)(1) only. It does not address licensed vocational nurses, certified nursing assistants, or other health care occupations that the subdivision does not name, and it does not state whether any particular nurse does or does not meet the executive or administrative criteria the subdivision refers to; the duties tests for those two exemptions appear in the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order and are the subject of a separate document in this corpus. The three advanced-practice-nurse categories to which section 515(f) does not apply are described in the next clause. The statute uses the phrase "he or she," which is reproduced in the quotation exactly as the posted text prints it.

THE THREE ADVANCED PRACTICE NURSE CATEGORIES SECTION 515(F) DOES NOT APPLY TO
Labor Code section 515(f)(2) states that subdivision (f) does not apply to three categories of certified nurses, each defined by the certification article of the Business and Professions Code that governs it: a certified nurse midwife primarily engaged in performing duties for which certification is required under Article 2.5 (commencing with Section 2746) of Chapter 6 of Division 2; a certified nurse anesthetist primarily engaged in performing duties for which certification is required under Article 7 (commencing with Section 2825) of that chapter; and a certified nurse practitioner primarily engaged in performing duties for which certification is required under Article 8 (commencing with Section 2834) of that chapter.

Section 515(f)(2)(D) then limits what that carve-out accomplishes. It states that nothing in the paragraph exempts those three occupations from meeting the requirements of subdivision (a). Removing the three categories from subdivision (f) therefore leaves them where every other candidate for the professional exemption stands: they must still satisfy section 515(a)'s conditions — primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customary and regular exercise of discretion and independent judgment, and the monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "(2) This subdivision does not apply to any of the following: (A) A certified nurse midwife who is primarily engaged in performing duties for which certification is required pursuant to Article 2.5 (commencing with Section 2746) of Chapter 6 of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code. (B) A certified nurse anesthetist who is primarily engaged in performing duties for which certification is required pursuant to Article 7 (commencing with Section 2825) of Chapter 6 of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code. (C) A certified nurse practitioner who is primarily engaged in performing duties for which certification is required pursuant to Article 8 (commencing with Section 2834) of Chapter 6 of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515(f)(2)(A)-(C) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.)
  "(D) Nothing in this paragraph shall exempt the occupations set forth in subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) from meeting the requirements of subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515(f)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515(f)(2)(D) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the text of section 515(f)(2) and does not determine whether any individual holds one of the three certifications it names or is "primarily engaged" in the certification-required duties, both of which are factual questions the statute leaves to application. The Business and Professions Code articles the statute cross-references are identified here by the numbers the Labor Code prints; their contents were not fetched or quoted for this document. The parallel provision in the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders, which states the same carve-out in regulatory form, is described in the following clause.

THE WAGE ORDER PROVISION THAT ADDS PHARMACISTS (WAGE ORDER 5-2001, SECTION 1(B)(3))
The Industrial Welfare Commission states the same rule in regulatory form, and states it for one occupation the Labor Code does not name. Section 1(B)(3)(f) of Wage Order 5-2001, the order for the public housekeeping industry, provides that notwithstanding the provisions of the professional-exemption subparagraph, pharmacists employed to engage in the practice of pharmacy and registered nurses employed to engage in the practice of nursing are not to be considered exempt professional employees, and are not to be considered exempt from coverage for purposes of that subsection, unless they individually meet the criteria established for exemption as executive or administrative employees.

Subparagraph (g) carries the advanced-practice-nurse carve-out, stating that subparagraph (f) does not apply to certified nurse midwives, certified nurse anesthetists, or certified nurse practitioners who are primarily engaged in performing duties for which the corresponding Business and Professions Code certification is required, and clause (iv) of that subparagraph states that nothing in it exempts those occupations from meeting the requirements of subsection 1(B)(3)(a)-(d) — the order's own duties, discretion, and salary requirements.

Wage Order 5-2001 reaches hospitals and similar institutions through its definition of the covered industry, which lists hospitals, sanitariums, rest homes, child nurseries, child care institutions, homes for the aged, and similar establishments offering board or lodging in addition to medical, surgical, nursing, convalescent, aged, or child care.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "(f) Notwithstanding the provisions of this subparagraph, pharmacists employed to engage in the practice of pharmacy, and registered nurses employed to engage in the practice of nursing, shall not be considered exempt professional employees, nor shall they be considered exempt from coverage for the purposes of this subsection unless they individually meet the criteria established for exemption as executive or administrative employees."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 5-2001, § 1(B)(3)(f) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11050, subd. 1(B)(3)(f) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle5.pdf)

  — IWC Wage Order No. 5-2001, § 1(B)(3)(g) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11050, subd. 1(B)(3)(g) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle5.pdf)
  "(iv) Nothing in this subparagraph shall exempt the occupations set forth in clauses (i), (ii), and (iii) from meeting the requirements of subsection 1(B)(3)(a)-(d), above."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 5-2001, § 1(B)(3)(g)(iv) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11050, subd. 1(B)(3)(g)(iv) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle5.pdf)
  "(4) Hospitals, sanitariums, rest homes, child nurseries, child care institutions, homes for the aged, and similar establishments offering board or lodging in addition to medical, surgical, nursing, convalescent, aged, or child care;"
  — IWC Wage Order No. 5-2001, § 2(P)(4) (California Department of Industrial Relations text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11050, subd. 2(P)(4) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle5.pdf)
  Known gap: Which of the Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders applies to a given employee depends on the employer's industry or the employee's occupation, and this document does not determine that question for any employer or employee; a pharmacist working in a retail setting, for example, may be covered by a different order than a pharmacist working in a hospital. Substantially parallel professional-exemption language, including the pharmacist and registered nurse sentence, appears in other wage orders, including Wage Order 4-2001; that parallel text is not quoted here because the text layer of the Department of Industrial Relations' Wage Order 4 PDF broke the sentence into out-of-order fragments in the extraction used to verify this document, so only the Wage Order 5 text — which the two independent fetches used for this document render contiguously — is quoted. The quotations below come from the Department of Industrial Relations' published PDF of the order; line-wrap hyphenation in the industry-definition quotation ("of-fering") was rejoined, and justified double spacing between words was collapsed. The order's section 1(B)(3)(a)-(d) requirements referred to in subparagraph (g)(iv) are not quoted in this document; this corpus addresses the wage orders' professional duties test separately.

THE PRIVATE ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOL TEACHER EXEMPTION (LABOR CODE SECTION 515.8)
Labor Code section 515.8(a) states that section 510 does not apply to an individual employed as a teacher at a private elementary or secondary academic institution in which pupils are enrolled in kindergarten or any of grades 1 to 12, inclusive.

Subdivision (b) supplies the definition that controls the exemption: for purposes of the section, "employed as a teacher" means that the employee meets all of the listed requirements. Two of them are duties requirements. The employee must be primarily engaged in the duty of imparting knowledge to pupils by teaching, instructing, or lecturing, and the employee must customarily and regularly exercise discretion and independent judgment in performing the duties of a teacher.

A fourth requirement is one of professional advancement: the employee must have attained either a baccalaureate or higher degree from an accredited institution of higher education, or current compliance with the requirements established by the California Commission on Teacher Credentialing, or the equivalent certification authority in another state, for obtaining a preliminary or alternative teaching credential. The third requirement, the salary floor, is the subject of the next clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "515.8. (a) Section 510 does not apply to an individual employed as a teacher at a private elementary or secondary academic institution in which pupils are enrolled in kindergarten or any of grades 1 to 12, inclusive."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.8(a) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.8(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.8.)
  "(b) For purposes of this section, “employed as a teacher” means that the employee meets all of the following requirements: (1) The employee is primarily engaged in the duty of imparting knowledge to pupils by teaching, instructing, or lecturing. (2) The employee customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing the duties of a teacher."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.8(b)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.8(b)(1)-(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.8.)
  "(4) The employee has attained at least one of the following levels of professional advancement: (A) A baccalaureate or higher degree from an accredited institution of higher education. (B) Current compliance with the requirements established by the California Commission on Teacher Credentialing, or the equivalent certification authority in another state, for obtaining a preliminary or alternative teaching credential."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.8(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.8(b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.8.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the text of section 515.8(a), (b)(1), (b)(2), and (b)(4). All of the requirements in subdivision (b) must be met together for an individual to be "employed as a teacher" within the meaning of the section, and this clause does not evaluate whether any particular teacher, including a person holding the position of Staff Physician, meets any of them. The section applies to private institutions enrolling pupils in kindergarten or grades 1 through 12; it does not by its terms address public school employees, whose hours and compensation are governed by other bodies of law this document does not describe, nor postsecondary institutions. The quotations below join line breaks the posted text places inside the statutory sentences.

THE TEACHER EXEMPTION’S SALARY FLOOR AND HOW IT IS MEASURED
The third requirement in Labor Code section 515.8(b) is a salary floor, and it is unusual among California's overtime exemptions because it is not measured against the state minimum wage. Under subdivision (b)(3), on and after July 1, 2017, a full-time employee must earn the greater of two amounts: no less than 100 percent of the lowest salary offered by any school district to a person in a position that requires a valid California teaching credential and who is not employed in that position pursuant to an emergency permit, intern permit, or waiver; or the equivalent of no less than 70 percent of the lowest schedule salary offered by the school district or county office of education in which the private institution is located to a person in such a credentialed position.

For a part-time employee, the statute requires the proportional amount of that salary, equal to the proportion of the full-time instructional schedule for which the part-time employee is employed.

Subdivision (c) addresses the timing problem this creates for a school setting its budget before public salary schedules for the coming year are known: when budgeting for a future school year, a private elementary or secondary academic institution may determine the salary requirements in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b) by referring to school salary schedules in effect for up to 12 months prior to the start of the school year.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "(3) On and after July 1, 2017, the employee earns the following amount: (A) For a full-time employee, the greater of the following: (i) No less than 100 percent of the lowest salary offered by any school district to a person who is in a position that requires the person to have a valid California teaching credential and is not employed in that position pursuant to an emergency permit, intern permit, or waiver. (ii) The equivalent of no less than 70 percent of the lowest schedule salary offered by the school district or the county office of education in which the private elementary or secondary academic institution is located to a person who is in a position that requires the person to have a valid California teaching credential and is not employed in that position pursuant to an emergency permit, intern permit, or waiver. (B) For a part-time employee, the proportional amount of the salary identified in subparagraph (A) that is equal to the proportion of the full-time instructional schedule for which the part-time employee is employed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.8(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.8(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.8.)
  "(c) When budgeting for a future school year, a private elementary or secondary academic institution may determine the salary requirements in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b) by referring to school salary schedules in effect for up to 12 months prior to the start of the school year."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.8(c) (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Lab. Code § 515.8(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.8.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the statutory text and does not perform the comparison the statute calls for. The two benchmarks in subdivision (b)(3)(A) are drawn from external sources — the salary schedules of California school districts and county offices of education — that change over time and vary by district; neither those schedules nor any resulting dollar figure was fetched, calculated, or reported for this document, and nothing here states what the applicable figure is for any institution or school year. The quotations below join line breaks the posted text places inside the statutory sentences.

SCHOOL EMPLOYEES THE TEACHER EXEMPTION EXCLUDES, AND ITS RELATIONSHIP TO THE WAGE ORDER EXEMPTIONS
Labor Code section 515.8(d) lists positions the section does not reach. It states that the section does not apply to any tutor, teaching assistant, instructional aide, student teacher, day care provider, vocational instructor, or other similar employee.

Subdivision (e) then describes how the section fits with the exemptions the Industrial Welfare Commission has established. It states that the exemption created in subdivision (a) is in addition to, and does not limit or supersede, any exemption from overtime established by a wage order of the commission for persons employed in a professional capacity, and that it does not affect any exemption from overtime established by that commission under subdivision (a) of section 515 for persons employed in an executive or administrative capacity. An employee who does not meet the section 515.8 definition is therefore not placed outside the wage orders' own executive, administrative, and professional exemptions by that fact; those exemptions are evaluated on their own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

expectedJSON.body:
Valley Medical Group, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe the occupation-specific overtime rules that California's Labor Code and the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders lay over the general professional exemption — the body of law that governs a position such as Staff Physician, held by Jordan Lee.

It describes the daily and weekly overtime requirement in Labor Code section 510 and the authority in section 515(a) under which the Industrial Welfare Commission establishes the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions; the separate hourly-rate exemption for licensed physicians and surgeons in section 515.6, the annual adjustment mechanism written into that section, and the rate the Department of Industrial Relations has most recently published under it; the two categories section 515.6 expressly does not reach, namely employees in a medical internship or resident program and physicians covered by a collective bargaining agreement meeting the conditions of section 514; section 515(f)'s rule that a registered nurse employed to engage in the practice of nursing is not exempted under the wage orders unless the nurse individually meets the executive or administrative criteria, and the three advanced-practice-nurse categories that rule does not apply to; the parallel provision in section 1(B)(3) of Wage Order 5-2001, which states the same rule for pharmacists employed to engage in the practice of pharmacy; and the separate exemption in section 515.8 for teachers at private elementary and secondary schools, with its duties requirements, its salary floor measured against public school district salary schedules, its degree-or-credential requirement, and the occupations it excludes.

This information sheet describes the law. It does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, does not evaluate any particular job or set of duties, does not calculate any employee's pay or overtime, and does not file anything with any agency or court.

California law requires overtime compensation for work beyond eight hours in a workday and beyond 40 hours in a workweek, and for the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in a workweek, at no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay, with a double-time requirement for work beyond 12 hours in a day (Labor Code section 510(a)).

Labor Code section 515(a) is the provision under which the Industrial Welfare Commission may establish exemptions from that requirement for executive, administrative, and professional employees, and by its terms it permits those exemptions only where the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment.

The provisions described in the rest of this document are occupation-specific rules that sit on top of that general framework. Two of them — sections 515.6 and 515.8 — are stand-alone statutory exemptions that state their own criteria and, by their own terms, make section 510 inapplicable to a defined group of employees. The others run the other direction: Labor Code section 515(f) and section 1(B)(3)(f) of Wage Order 5-2001 state that particular licensed occupations are not covered by the professional exemption at all unless the employee separately meets the executive or administrative criteria.

Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee.

Labor Code section 515(f)(1) addresses registered nurses directly. It states that, in addition to the requirements of subdivision (a), a registered nurse employed to engage in the practice of nursing is not exempted from coverage under the orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission unless the nurse individually meets the criteria for exemptions established for executive or administrative employees.

The structure of that sentence matters. It does not create an exemption; it closes one. The only route to exempt status the subdivision leaves open is the executive or administrative route, and it requires that the individual nurse meet those criteria — which, under section 515(a), include being primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercising discretion and independent judgment, and earning the required salary.

Labor Code section 515.8(a) states that section 510 does not apply to an individual employed as a teacher at a private elementary or secondary academic institution in which pupils are enrolled in kindergarten or any of grades 1 to 12, inclusive.

Subdivision (b) supplies the definition that controls the exemption: for purposes of the section, "employed as a teacher" means that the employee meets all of the listed requirements. Two of them are duties requirements. The employee must be primarily engaged in the duty of imparting knowledge to pupils by teaching, instructing, or lecturing, and the employee must customarily and regularly exercise discretion and independent judgment in performing the duties of a teacher.

A fourth requirement is one of professional advancement: the employee must have attained either a baccalaureate or higher degree from an accredited institution of higher education, or current compliance with the requirements established by the California Commission on Teacher Credentialing, or the equivalent certification authority in another state, for obtaining a preliminary or alternative teaching credential. The third requirement, the salary floor, is the subject of the next clause.

The third requirement in Labor Code section 515.8(b) is a salary floor, and it is unusual among California's overtime exemptions because it is not measured against the state minimum wage. Under subdivision (b)(3), on and after July 1, 2017, a full-time employee must earn the greater of two amounts: no less than 100 percent of the lowest salary offered by any school district to a person in a position that requires a valid California teaching credential and who is not employed in that position pursuant to an emergency permit, intern permit, or waiver; or the equivalent of no less than 70 percent of the lowest schedule salary offered by the school district or county office of education in which the private institution is located to a person in such a credentialed position.

For a part-time employee, the statute requires the proportional amount of that salary, equal to the proportion of the full-time instructional schedule for which the part-time employee is employed.

Subdivision (c) addresses the timing problem this creates for a school setting its budget before public salary schedules for the coming year are known: when budgeting for a future school year, a private elementary or secondary academic institution may determine the salary requirements in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b) by referring to school salary schedules in effect for up to 12 months prior to the start of the school year.
